questions.q: Why doesn't LDA simply choose the direction along which the two class **centres** are furthest apart?
options: Because each class may be widely spread along that same direction, so the classes still overlap; LDA maximises the gap **relative to** the within-class spread
Because the centres are unknown until after projection
Because LDA ignores the class labels
Because the furthest-apart direction is always one of the original features
questions.why: Fisher's ratio divides the squared gap between projected means by the projected within-class spread. Long, thin classes stretched along the centre-to-centre line overlap badly there, so LDA may prefer an angle where the centres are a bit closer but each class looks much narrower. LDA is supervised: it needs the labels to compute class means at all.

questions.q: Two classes along one feature have means **20** and **36** and the same spread. With **equal priors**, where does LDA put the cut-off?
options: It depends on the number of features
questions.why: With equal priors the log term vanishes and the cut-off is the midpoint of the means: (20 + 36) / 2 = 28. 16 is the gap between the means, not the midpoint. Unequal priors would shift the cut towards the rarer class.

questions.q: DTI example: repaid customers average 30%, defaulters 50%, shared SD 10. Now only **10%** of customers default. Using **cut-off = (μ₁ + μ₂)/2 + σ² ln(π₂/π₁) / (μ₁ − μ₂)** with repaid as class 1, where is the cut-off?
options: About 51.0%
About 46.9%
About 29.0%
questions.why: Shift = 100 × ln(0.1 / 0.9) / (30 − 50) = 100 × (−2.197) / (−20) ≈ +10.99, so the cut-off ≈ 40 + 11.0 = 51.0%, beyond even the defaulters' average. 46.9% is the answer for the chapter's 20% default rate; 40% ignores the priors; 29.0% shifts the cut the wrong way, towards the common class.

questions.q: In the six-point example, Fisher's direction gives the score **−5 × feature 1 + 4 × feature 2**, with class A scoring above the cut-off of **−5** and class B below it. Which class does LDA give a new point at **(4, 4)**?
options: Class B, because feature 1 = 4 is a typical class-B value
Class B, because its score is −4, which is negative
Class A, because its score is −20 + 16 = −4, above the cut-off of −5
Neither: the point lies exactly on the boundary
questions.why: Score = −5 × 4 + 4 × 4 = −4, which is above −5, so class A. Judging by feature 1 alone is exactly what LDA improves on: the two classes overlap on that feature. A negative score does not mean class B; what matters is which side of the cut-off it falls.

questions.q: Why are LDA's boundaries straight, and what changes in **QDA**?
options: LDA uses only one feature; QDA uses many
LDA uses gradient descent; QDA uses a closed form
LDA assumes every class shares the same covariance, which makes the class scores linear in x; QDA lets each class have its own covariance, giving curved boundaries at the cost of many more parameters
LDA ignores priors; QDA includes them
questions.why: With a shared spread, the squared terms in each class's bell curve cancel when you compare classes, leaving straight-line scores. Separate spreads keep those terms, so the boundary curves. Both use priors, and both are fitted from means and covariances without iterative search.

questions.q: With the real 80/20 priors, LDA gives the DTI-44% applicant a default probability of about **0.36** and predicts "repaid". A missed default costs the lender far more than a lost good customer. What should the lender do?
options: Accept "repaid", because LDA's prediction already accounts for priors
Set the priors to 50/50 to force more defaults
Drop LDA because 0.36 is too uncertain
Keep the LDA probabilities but set a lower decision threshold on them (well below 0.5) to reflect the costs
questions.why: Priors make the probability honest about how common defaults are; costs are a separate business input applied through the threshold. Faking equal priors distorts the probabilities to sneak in a cost judgement. A 0.36 chance of default is useful information, not a failure.

questions.q: A dataset contains two features that are exact copies of each other, and LDA fails with a numerical error. Why, and what is the fix?
options: LDA cannot handle more than two features; drop one at random
The class means become equal; standardise the features
The priors are undefined; set them manually
The within-class scatter matrix S_W cannot be inverted when features are perfect duplicates; remove the duplicate or use shrinkage (`solver="lsqr", shrinkage="auto"`)
questions.why: Fisher's direction is w ∝ S_W⁻¹(μ_A − μ_B), and duplicate columns make S_W singular, the matrix equivalent of dividing by zero. Shrinkage stabilises S_W, which also helps when there are many features and few rows. Standardising does not remove a perfect duplicate.

questions.q: Interview question: "LDA and logistic regression both draw straight boundaries. When would you prefer each?"
options: LDA is more efficient with small samples when classes are roughly normal with similar spread; logistic regression is safer when those assumptions fail and usually gives better-calibrated probabilities on larger data
Always LDA, because it is older and better understood
Always logistic regression, because LDA cannot output probabilities
LDA for regression problems and logistic regression for classification
questions.why: LDA is generative: it models each class as a bell curve and uses Bayes' theorem, which pays off with little data if the model is right. Logistic regression models only the log-odds and makes no assumption about the feature distributions. LDA does produce probabilities, but they can be overconfident when normality is badly wrong.
